paragraphs: The very existence of the Greek state is today threatened by the terrorist activities of several thousand armed men, led by Communists, who defy the government's authority at a number of points, particularly along the northern boundaries. …

The British Government, which has been helping Greece, can give no further financial or economic aid after March 31. Great Britain finds itself under the necessity of reducing or liquidating its commitments in several parts of the world, including Greece. …
At the present moment in world history nearly every nation must choose between alternative ways of life. The choice is too often not a free one.

One way of life is based upon the will of the majority, and is distinguished by free institutions, representative government, free elections, guarantees of individual liberty, freedom of speech and religion, and freedom from political oppression.

The second way of life is based upon the will of a minority forcibly imposed upon the majority. It relies upon terror and oppression, a controlled press and radio; fixed elections, and the suppression of personal freedoms.

I believe that it must be the policy of the United States to support free peoples who are resisting attempted subjugation by armed minorities or by outside pressures. … I believe that our help should be primarily through economic and financial aid which is essential to economic stability and orderly political processes. …
I therefore ask the Congress to provide authority for assistance to Greece and Turkey in the amount of $400,000,000 for the period ending June 30, 1948.

paragraphs: As I read your letter, the key elements of your proposals—which seem generally acceptable as I understand them—are as follows: 1) You would agree to remove these weapons systems from Cuba under appropriate United Nations observation and supervision; and undertake, with suitable safeguards, to halt the further introduction of such weapons systems into Cuba. 2) We, on our part, would agree … (a) to remove promptly the quarantine measures now in effect and (b) to give assurances against an invasion of Cuba. …

But the first ingredient, let me emphasize, is the cessation of work on missile sites in Cuba and measures to render such weapons inoperable, under effective international guarantees. The continuation of this threat, or a prolonging of this discussion concerning Cuba by linking these problems to the broader questions of European and world security, would surely lead to an intensification of the Cuban crisis and a grave risk to the peace of the world.

paragraphs: In August 1945, the Japanese surrendered to the Allies. The popular forces of Vietnam which, since 1940, had made incessant attacks on the Japanese forces, … went down to conquer the capital-city and the governing rule. … On September 2, 1945, the Democratic Republic of Vietnam was solemnly proclaimed. … The new Republic of Vietnam, thus legally instituted, is in the reconstruction of the world a factor of peace and progress. She is entitled for her safeguard to refer to the most sacred principles of SAN FRANCISCO and ATLANTIC Charters*. She is based on and draws her strength from, the first of SUN YAT SEN's Three Principles and the second, fourth, sixth points of President TRUMAN's twelve-point declaration.

But, on September 23, 1945, the French troops attacked Saigon, starting an invasion which is now in its fifth month. That invasion is menacing North Vietnam … . That aggression, carried on by an experienced and numerous army, fully equipped with the most recent inventions of modern warfare, has brought about the destruction of our towns and villages, the assassination of our civilian population, the starving of a great part of our country. …

First of all, democracy has been established on solid foundations. On January 6 last, general elections were organized with the greatest success. … A new administrative organization has replaced the old mandarinate system. The most unpopular taxes have been abolished. The anti-illiteracy campaign organized along efficient lines, has yielded unexpectedly optimistic results. …

For those reasons, we think it our duty to send this note to the Great Powers—which had led the anti-fascist crusade to final victory … . While waiting with confidence for a positive measure from the Governments of WASHINGTON, MOSCOW, LONDON, and CHUNGKING, we have determined to fight to our last drop of blood against the reestablishment of French imperialism. … We only ask full independence, independence that is so far a fact, and that will enable us to cooperate with the other nations in the building-up of a better world and lasting peace.

paragraphs: In the year 1949, after more than a century of heroic struggle, the Chinese people, led by the Communist Party of China, finally achieved their great victory in the people's revolution against imperialism, feudalism and bureaucrat-capitalism; and so brought to an end a long history of oppression and enslavement and founded the People's Republic of China, a people's democratic dictatorship. …

From the founding of the People's Republic of China to the attainment of a socialist society is a period of transition. During the transition the fundamental task of the state is, step by step, to bring about the socialist industrialization of the country and, step by step, to accomplish the socialist transformation of agriculture, handicrafts and capitalist industry and commerce. In the last few years our people have successfully carried out a series of large-scale struggles: the reform of the agrarian system, resistance to American aggression and aid to Korea, the suppression of counter-revolutionaries and the rehabilitation of the national economy. …

China has already built an indestructible friendship with the great Union of Soviet Socialist Republics and the People's Democracies; and the friendship between our people and peace-loving people in all other countries is growing day by day. …

paragraphs: We face a hostile ideology—global in scope, atheistic in character, ruthless in purpose, and insidious in method. Unhappily the danger it poses promises to be of indefinite duration. …

Until the latest of our world conflicts, the United States had no armaments industry. American makers of plowshares could, with time and as required, make swords as well. But now we can no longer risk emergency improvisation of national defense; we have been compelled to create a permanent armaments industry of vast proportions. Added to this, three and a half million men and women are directly engaged in the defense establishment. We annually spend on military security more than the net income of all United States corporations.

This conjunction of an immense military establishment and a large arms industry is new in the American experience. The total influence—economic, political, even spiritual—is felt in every city, every State house, every office of the Federal government. … In the councils of government, we must guard against the acquisition of unwarranted influence, whether sought or unsought, by the military-industrial complex. The potential for the disastrous rise of misplaced power exists and will persist. …
Disarmament, with mutual honor and confidence, is a continuing imperative. … I confess that I lay down my official responsibilities in this field with a definite sense of disappointment.

paragraphs: The absolute equality of races,—physical, political and social—is the founding stone of world peace and human advancement. …

The beginning of wisdom in interracial contact is the establishment of political institutions among suppressed peoples. The habit of democracy must be made to encircle the earth. … Local self-government with a minimum of help and oversight can be established tomorrow in Asia, in Africa, in America and in the Isles of the Sea. …

England, with her Pax Britannica, her courts of justice, established commerce and a certain apparent recognition of native law and customs, has nevertheless systematically fostered ignorance among the natives, … has usually declined even to try to train black and brown men in real self-government, to recognize civilized black folks as civilized, or to grant to colored colonies those rights of self-government which it freely gives to white men. …
The Negro* race through its thinking intelligentsia is demanding:

I—The recognition of civilized men as civilized despite their race or color
II—Local self government for backward groups, deliberately rising as experience and knowledge grow to complete self government under the limitations of a self governed world
… VI—The ancient common ownership of the land and its natural fruits and defence against the unrestrained greed of invested capital
VII—The establishment under the League of Nations of an international institution for the study of Negro problems

paragraphs: At bottom of Kremlin's neurotic view of world affairs is traditional and instinctive Russian sense of insecurity. … Russian rulers have invariably sensed that their rule was relatively archaic in form, fragile and artificial in its psychological foundation, unable to stand comparison or contact with political systems of Western countries. For this reason they have always feared foreign penetration … . And they have learned to seek security only in patient but deadly struggle for total destruction of rival power, never in compacts and compromises with it. …

(1) Soviet power, unlike that of Hitlerite Germany, is neither schematic nor adventuristic. It does not work by fixed plans. It does not take unnecessary risks. Impervious to logic of reason, and it is highly sensitive to logic of force. For this reason it can easily withdraw—and usually does—when strong resistance is encountered at any point. …

(2) Gauged against Western World as a whole, Soviets are still by far the weaker force. Thus, their success will really depend on degree of cohesion, firmness and vigor which Western World can muster. …
… World communism is like malignant parasite which feeds only on diseased tissue. This is point at which domestic and foreign policies meet. …

paragraphs: In considering the requirements for the rehabilitation of Europe, the physical loss of life, the visible destruction of cities, factories, mines, and railroads was correctly estimated, but it has become obvious during recent months that this visible destruction was probably less serious than the dislocation of the entire fabric of European economy. …

The truth of the matter is that Europe's requirements for the next three or four years of foreign food and other essential products—principally from America—are so much greater than her present ability to pay that she must have substantial additional help or face economic, social, and political deterioration of a very grave character. …

Our policy is directed not against any country or doctrine but against hunger, poverty, desperation, and chaos. Its purpose should be the revival of a working economy in the world so as to permit the emergence of political and social conditions in which free institutions can exist. … Any government which maneuvers to block the recovery of other countries cannot expect help from us. Furthermore, governments, political parties, or groups which seek to perpetuate human misery in order to profit therefrom politically or otherwise will encounter the opposition of the United States.
… The initiative, I think, must come from Europe. … The program should be a joint one, agreed to by a number, if not all, European nations.

paragraphs: On June 17, 1952, a comprehensive agrarian reform program became law in Guatemala. Its professed objective is the development of a capitalistic agricultural economy through the abolition of semi-feudal owner-worker relationships, the redistribution of land, and the improvement with state assistance of cultivation methods. The implications of the legislation, however, go beyond agrarian reform inasmuch as its provisions furnish a basis for the strengthening of political and Communist control over the rural population.

Full implementation of the law would free thousands of agrarian workers from a centuries-old dependence upon the privileged landholding class, but would subject the majority, in all probability, to close control by the state. …

Administration forces undoubtedly envisage political benefits from the legislation. They are presumably anxious to break the control of the conservative anti-administration large landholders over the farm labor force in order to organize it behind the government. Advantages to the Communists are likely to be enhanced by the opportunity to extend the influence in farm areas … and through greater opportunities to attack the United Fruit Company. …

… The extent to which land controlled by foreign agriculture corporations may be made available for redistribution is largely a matter of speculation. Largest of these enterprises is the United Fruit Company which owns or leases some 450,000 acres possibly subject to expropriation.

paragraphs: … I wanted to avoid violence, I want to avoid violence. Non-violence is the first article of my faith. It is also the last article of my creed. …

The first shock came in the shape of the Rowlatt Act, a law designed to rob the people of all real freedom. I felt called upon to lead an intensive agitation against it. Then followed the Punjab horrors beginning with the massacre at Jallianwala Bagh and culminating in crawling orders, public flogging and other indescribable humiliations. …

I came reluctantly to the conclusion that the British connection had made India more helpless than she ever was before, politically and economically. … Before the British advent, India spun and wove in her millions of cottages just the supplement she needed for adding to her meagre agricultural resources. This cottage industry, so vital for India's existence, has been ruined by incredibly heartless and inhuman processes as described by English witnesses. …

In my humble opinion, Non-co-operation with evil is as much a duty as is co-operation with good. But in the past, Non-co-operation has been deliberately expressed in violence to the evil doer. I am endeavouring to show to my countrymen that violent Non-co-operation only multiplies evil and that as evil can only be sustained by violence, withdrawal of support of evil requires complete abstention from violence. Non-violence implies voluntary submission to the penalty for Non-co-operation with evil. I am here, therefore, to invite and submit cheerfully to the highest penalty that can be inflicted upon me for what in law is a deliberate crime and what appears to me to be the highest duty of a citizen.

practice.stem: The manifesto was most likely written in response to which of the following?

options.A: the Atlantic Charter's promise that peoples could choose their own form of government
options.B: the May Fourth Movement, in which Chinese students protested the transfer of Germany's rights in Shandong to Japan
options.C: Italy's conquest of Ethiopia, one of Africa's last independent states
options.D: a peace settlement after the First World War that maintained European colonial rule over most of Africa

practice.explanation: After the First World War, the peace treaties handed Germany's colonies to Britain, France, and others as mandates. Africans and Asians who had hoped for more self-rule were let down. Meetings like the Pan-African Congress spoke out against this.

whyNot.A: Roosevelt and Churchill issued the Atlantic Charter in 1941, twenty years after this manifesto.
whyNot.B: The May Fourth protests of 1919 answered the same peace treaty, but they were about China. The manifesto speaks for Africans and people of African descent.
whyNot.C: Italy invaded Ethiopia in 1935, more than ten years after this manifesto.

practice.hint: What had happened in world politics just a few years before 1921?

practice.stem: Point II of the manifesto argues for

options.A: a path that would lead colonized peoples step by step toward full self-government
options.B: an armed revolt that would drive the colonial powers out of Africa as soon as possible
options.C: the return of people of African descent in the Americas to a homeland in Africa
options.D: League of Nations rule over Africa in place of rule by the colonial powers

practice.explanation: Point II asks for local self-government that would grow "as experience and knowledge grow" until it became complete. Many early leaders hoped to reach self-rule through reform, a little at a time.

whyNot.B: The manifesto asks for self-government that keeps "rising" over time. It does not call for revolt.
whyNot.C: Marcus Garvey called for a return to Africa in these years, but the manifesto does not.
whyNot.D: Point VII asks the League to set up a body to study problems, not to govern Africa.

practice.hint: Reread point II slowly. What would come first, and what would come later?

practice.stem: Which statement in the manifesto most directly supports its criticism that British colonial policy treated racial groups unequally?

options.A: Britain brought courts of justice and trade to its colonies.
options.B: Britain gave some recognition to native law and customs.
options.C: The League of Nations should set up an institution to study problems facing people of African descent.
options.D: Britain denied colonized peoples rights of self-government that it granted to white populations.

practice.explanation: Choice D directly compares how Britain treated colonized peoples with how it treated white populations. The manifesto says Britain refused "to grant to colored colonies those rights of self-government which it freely gives to white men." The other statements are concessions the manifesto makes about British rule or a recommendation, not evidence of unequal treatment.

whyNot.A: The manifesto grants that Britain set up courts and trade, but says it "nevertheless" kept colonized peoples from self-government. This is a concession, not evidence of unequal treatment.
whyNot.B: The manifesto calls this recognition only "apparent." It is a concession, not evidence that Britain treated racial groups unequally.
whyNot.C: This is a recommendation for the League of Nations, not evidence about Britain's treatment of racial groups.

practice.hint: Separate evidence that supports a claim from a goal or a recommendation.

practice.stem: Kennan's main purpose in writing the telegram was most likely to

options.A: explain Soviet behavior to U.S. leaders and urge firm resistance to it
options.B: propose that the United States and the Soviet Union share control of atomic weapons
options.C: warn U.S. leaders that the Soviet Union was about to attack Western Europe
options.D: argue that the West should pull its forces out of Europe and trust the Soviets to keep the peace

practice.explanation: Kennan wanted Washington to understand why Soviet leaders acted as they did. He argued that the Soviets would back down when they met strong resistance. His ideas became the basis of containment.

whyNot.B: Kennan says the Soviets respond to the "logic of force." He does not suggest sharing weapons.
whyNot.C: Kennan says Soviet power "does not take unnecessary risks" and can be checked without war.
whyNot.D: Kennan says Soviet success depends on the West's "cohesion, firmness and vigor." He does not want the West to pull back.

practice.hint: Who received the telegram, and what does Kennan say will make the Soviets back down?

practice.stem: Ideas like Kennan's contributed most directly to which U.S. policy?

options.A: détente, which aimed to ease tensions through arms control and trade with the Soviets
options.B: isolationism, which aimed to keep the United States out of European affairs
options.C: containment, which aimed to stop the spread of Soviet power and communism
options.D: appeasement, which aimed to keep the peace by giving in to a rival's demands

practice.explanation: In 1947 Kennan published his ideas in a magazine article. The Truman Doctrine and the Marshall Plan put containment into action. It guided U.S. policy for the rest of the Cold War.

whyNot.A: Détente, an effort to ease Cold War tensions, came mainly in the late 1960s and 1970s. Kennan's telegram called for firmness.
whyNot.B: Kennan argues that the United States must stay involved and resist Soviet power abroad.
whyNot.D: Appeasement was the 1930s policy toward Hitler. Kennan says the Soviets respond to strength.

practice.hint: Think about when each policy was used and whom it was aimed at.

practice.stem: Which of the following events would best support Kennan's claim that Soviet power "can easily withdraw … when strong resistance is encountered"?

options.A: Soviet tanks crushed an uprising against communist rule in Hungary.
options.B: The Soviet Union tested its first atomic bomb in 1949, years before American experts had expected.
options.C: The Soviets lifted their blockade of West Berlin after a Western airlift supplied the city.
options.D: North Korea, backed by the Soviet Union, invaded South Korea.

practice.explanation: The Soviets cut the roads and railways into West Berlin in 1948. The United States and Britain flew in food and fuel for almost a year. In May 1949 the Soviets gave up the blockade.

whyNot.A: In Hungary the Soviets used force and did not back down. The West did not send troops to stop them.
whyNot.B: The bomb test showed growing Soviet strength. It does not show a Soviet retreat.
whyNot.D: The invasion was a push forward, not a withdrawal.

practice.hint: Look for an event in which the Soviets met resistance and then backed down.

practice.stem: Marshall's description of Europe's economy is best understood in the context of

options.A: the Great Depression, which had left Europe's farmers and factories unable to sell their goods in the 1930s
options.B: the damage done by the Second World War, which left the United States the strongest economy
options.C: the founding of the European Economic Community, which had removed trade barriers in Europe
options.D: the Allied occupation of Germany, during which the Soviets took factories and machines from their zone

practice.explanation: The war wrecked Europe's cities, factories, and trade. Most U.S. factories came through the war intact, and the United States had the largest economy in the world. That is why Marshall says Europe needed goods "principally from America."

whyNot.A: The Depression began in 1929. Marshall describes destroyed cities, factories, and railroads, which point to the war that had ended in 1945.
whyNot.C: The European Economic Community was founded in 1957, ten years after this speech.
whyNot.D: The Soviets took machines mainly from their own zone of Germany and received some from the western zones. Reparations alone do not explain the wider damage and broken trade that Marshall describes.

practice.hint: Check the date of each choice against June 1947. Which one explains both Europe's broken economy and its need for goods 'principally from America'?

practice.stem: Marshall's warning about "political parties … which seek to perpetuate human misery" most likely referred to

options.A: fascist parties in Germany and Italy that were planning to return to power
options.B: Communist parties in Western Europe, such as those in France and Italy
options.C: nationalist parties in Asia and Africa that wanted to end European rule
options.D: Britain's Labour Party, which wanted the government to run key industries

practice.explanation: Communist parties won large shares of the vote in France and Italy after the war. U.S. leaders feared that hunger and unemployment would help them take power. Aid was meant to remove that danger.

whyNot.A: Marshall's warning reflected U.S. concern about strong Communist parties in postwar Europe. The defeated wartime fascist regimes were not the main target of this warning.
whyNot.C: Marshall is speaking about Europe's recovery, not about colonies in Asia and Africa.
whyNot.D: Britain's Labour government welcomed Marshall's offer and received more aid than any other country.

practice.hint: Check each choice: was that party strong in Western Europe in 1947, and did U.S. leaders oppose it?

practice.stem: The Soviet Union responded to the program Marshall proposed by

options.A: joining the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank to get Western loans for rebuilding
options.B: offering loans and experts to newly independent states such as India and Egypt
options.C: forming the Warsaw Pact, a military alliance with the communist states of Eastern Europe
options.D: refusing the aid, keeping Eastern Europe out of it, and setting up its own economic council

practice.explanation: Stalin saw the Marshall Plan as a way for the United States to gain influence in Europe. He made Poland and Czechoslovakia turn it down. In 1949 the Soviets set up the Council for Mutual Economic Assistance (Comecon) to tie Eastern Europe's economies to their own.

whyNot.A: The Soviets helped plan these institutions in 1944, but they did not join them.
whyNot.B: Soviet aid to India and Egypt began in the mid-1950s. It was not an answer to aid for Europe.
whyNot.C: The Warsaw Pact came in 1955, after West Germany joined NATO. It was a military alliance, not an answer to economic aid.

practice.hint: Check the date of each choice. Which one came soon after 1947 and dealt with Europe's economy?

practice.stem: The treaty's concern about a "remilitarized West Germany" is best understood in the context of

options.A: the Treaty of Versailles, which had limited the size of Germany's army after the First World War
options.B: Germany's invasion of the Soviet Union in the Second World War, in which more than 20 million Soviet people died
options.C: the Marshall Plan, which sent American aid to rebuild West Germany's factories and cities
options.D: the Berlin Wall, which East Germany built to stop its people from fleeing to the West

practice.explanation: In 1941 Germany invaded the Soviet Union. More than 20 million Soviet people died, and Poland and other Eastern European lands were also devastated. Ten years after the war, the Soviets and their allies feared a rearmed Germany. West Germany joined NATO in May 1955, and the Soviet bloc signed this treaty about a week later.

whyNot.A: Versailles limited Germany's army in 1919. It does not explain why Germany's eastern neighbors feared a new German army in 1955.
whyNot.C: The Marshall Plan was economic aid. The treaty worries about German soldiers, not German factories.
whyNot.D: The Berlin Wall was built in 1961, six years after this treaty.

practice.hint: Ask why the Soviet Union and Poland in particular would fear a German army in 1955.

practice.stem: Which of the following later developments would most directly challenge the treaty's promise of "non-intervention in each other's domestic affairs"?

options.A: In the 1960s Romania traded more with Western Europe and took its own positions on foreign affairs.
options.B: In 1968 troops from the Soviet Union and several other member states invaded Czechoslovakia to end its reforms.
options.C: In 1979 Soviet troops invaded Afghanistan to support its communist government.
options.D: In 1984 the Soviet Union and most of its allies kept their athletes home from the Olympic Games in Los Angeles.

practice.explanation: In 1968 Czechoslovakia's Communist leader, Alexander Dubček, allowed more free speech in the "Prague Spring." Soviet leaders feared the reforms would spread. Troops from the Soviet Union, Poland, Hungary, and Bulgaria invaded and ended them. Afterward the Soviets claimed a right to step in wherever communist rule was "threatened," an idea called the Brezhnev Doctrine.

whyNot.A: Romania's moves show a member acting on its own. They do not show other members interfering in its affairs.
whyNot.C: Afghanistan did not belong to the Warsaw Pact, so this promise among members did not cover it.
whyNot.D: The boycott was a joint protest against the United States. It was not an invasion of a member country.

practice.hint: Check each choice: was the country involved a member of the treaty, and did other countries step into its affairs?

practice.stem: A historian investigating how much independence the Eastern European member governments had in practice would find the treaty limited chiefly because

options.A: it states the members' official promises but cannot show whether those promises were kept
options.B: it presents West Germany's rearmament and entry into NATO as a threat to the security of the member states
options.C: it provides for military coordination among countries with different national histories
options.D: it connects military cooperation with promises of economic and cultural cooperation

practice.explanation: The treaty records the alliance's public commitments, including respect for each member's independence. It cannot by itself show how much freedom member governments had in practice. Records of Soviet pressure, talks among member governments, and military interventions would help a historian test those commitments.

whyNot.B: This shows the alliance's stated security concern. It does not show whether members respected one another's independence.
whyNot.C: Military coordination can happen under different relationships among governments. It does not show how freely each government made decisions.
whyNot.D: Promises of cooperation do not show whether members kept their independence in making decisions.

practice.hint: Ask what kind of document a treaty is. What can it show, and what can it not show?

practice.stem: The law was issued in the context of

options.A: the Communist Party's victory over the Nationalists in China's civil war
options.B: the Long March, when Communist forces retreated across China to escape the Nationalist army
options.C: the Hundred Flowers campaign, when the party briefly invited people to criticize its rule
options.D: Japan's invasion of China, when the Communists and Nationalists formed a united front

practice.explanation: After Japan's defeat in 1945, full-scale civil war resumed between Mao's Communists and Chiang Kai-shek's Nationalists. The Communists won and founded the People's Republic of China in October 1949, and the Nationalists fled to Taiwan. This land law was one of the new government's first big laws.

whyNot.B: The Long March took place in 1934–1935, when the Communists held only small areas of China.
whyNot.C: The Hundred Flowers campaign came in 1956–1957, six years after this law.
whyNot.D: Japan's full-scale war against China began in 1937, after its seizure of Manchuria in 1931. Japan's defeat in 1945 came before this law, and Communist-Nationalist cooperation had already collapsed.

practice.hint: Look at the date of the law. Which choice describes events in China at that time?

practice.stem: Land reform under this law most directly helped the new Communist government by

options.A: paying landlords for their land with bonds and shares in state companies, as the Nationalists did on Taiwan
options.B: forcing peasant families to pool their land and labor in collective farms, as the Soviet Union had done
options.C: winning the support of poor peasants and breaking the power of landlords in the villages
options.D: gaining help from the United States, which wanted China's peasants to own their own land

practice.explanation: Most Chinese were poor farmers. Giving them landlords' land won the new government their support, and village meetings broke the landlords' power. Although Article 32 forbids "indiscriminate … killing," land reform campaigns included public humiliation, beatings, and executions of people identified as landlords.

whyNot.A: Article 2 says the landlords' land was confiscated, not bought. The Nationalists' land reform on Taiwan in 1953 did pay landlords.
whyNot.B: Article 1 introduces peasant landownership, and Article 10 gives confiscated land to peasants. China's drive to organize farming into collective farms came later in the 1950s.
whyNot.D: The United States backed land reform in Japan and Taiwan, but it did not aid Communist China, which it saw as an enemy.

practice.hint: Test each choice against Articles 1, 2, and 10. Which one matches what the law actually did?

practice.stem: The law's plan to give confiscated land to "poor peasants who have little or no land" is most similar to which other twentieth-century development?

options.A: land reform after the Mexican Revolution, which broke up large estates and gave land to peasant villages
options.B: the Green Revolution, which spread new high-yield seeds and chemical fertilizers to farmers in India and Mexico
options.C: Stalin's collectivization, which forced Soviet peasants to give up their own plots and join large farms
options.D: laws in South Africa that set aside most of the country's land for white farmers

practice.explanation: After the Mexican Revolution, the 1917 constitution let the government break up large estates, called haciendas. In the 1930s President Lázaro Cárdenas gave millions of acres to peasant villages. Like the Chinese law, Mexico's reform took land from big owners and gave it to the poor.

whyNot.B: The Green Revolution raised harvests with new seeds and fertilizer. It did not take land from big owners.
whyNot.C: Collectivization took land away from peasant families. This law gave land to them.
whyNot.D: These laws took land from the Black majority for a white minority. This law gave land to the poor majority.

practice.hint: Reread what should happen to the landlords' property. Then ask what each choice did to who owned the land.

practice.stem: The law described in the report is an example of

options.A: liberal reforms of the 1800s that sold church and village lands to private buyers
options.B: the encomienda system, under which Spanish colonists were given the labor of Native Americans
options.C: a land plan required by the Alliance for Progress to build farm cooperatives
options.D: movements in Latin America to redistribute land, sometimes with socialist support

practice.explanation: In much of Latin America, a few families and companies owned most of the good land. Árbenz's government set out to break up large estates and give unused land to peasants. Guatemala's small Communist Party supported the reform, but land redistribution did not by itself make Guatemala a Communist state.

whyNot.A: Those reforms moved land into private hands, often big estates. This law takes land from big estates.
whyNot.B: The encomienda system belonged to Spain's colonial rule in the 1500s. This law aimed to end "semi-feudal" ties between landowners and workers.
whyNot.C: The Alliance for Progress began in 1961, nine years after this law.

practice.hint: What does the law do with land owned by large estates?

practice.stem: The report's concern that the law could strengthen "Communist control" most likely reflects

options.A: a hope among U.S. officials that breaking up large estates would make Guatemala more democratic and stable
options.B: the Good Neighbor Policy's stated commitment to avoid military intervention in Latin America
options.C: U.S. support for land reform in Japan, which American occupation officials carried out after the war
options.D: a Cold War fear among U.S. officials that reforms nearby could open the door to Soviet influence

practice.explanation: In the early 1950s, U.S. leaders saw communism as a worldwide threat. When Guatemala's government passed a land law backed by its small Communist Party, U.S. officials saw a danger close to home.

whyNot.A: The report worries that the law puts workers under "close control by the state."
whyNot.B: The Good Neighbor Policy stressed nonintervention. This report shows how Cold War fears could conflict with that promise.
whyNot.C: The United States did back land reform in occupied Japan, but this report worries that Guatemala's reform would help Communists.

practice.hint: Check each choice against the words of the report and the year it was written.

practice.stem: Which later U.S. action most directly addressed the concerns about Guatemala expressed in the report?

options.A: the Bay of Pigs invasion, in which Cuban exiles trained by the CIA landed in Cuba
options.B: the Roosevelt Corollary, under which the United States claimed the right to act as a police power in Latin America
options.C: a CIA-backed overthrow of the Árbenz government
options.D: the founding of the Organization of American States to settle disputes among countries in the Americas

practice.explanation: In 1954 the CIA armed and trained Guatemalan exiles led by Carlos Castillo Armas, ran a propaganda radio station, and supplied planes that bombed targets in Guatemala. Árbenz resigned, Castillo Armas took power, and his government gave land back to United Fruit. A civil war followed from 1960 to 1996, in which about 200,000 people were killed or disappeared, most of them Maya.

whyNot.A: The Bay of Pigs invasion targeted Castro's government in Cuba in 1961. The intervention in Guatemala in choice C is the more direct connection to the government and concerns in this report.
whyNot.B: The Roosevelt Corollary dates from 1904, long before this 1953 report.
whyNot.D: The OAS was founded in 1948, five years before this report.

practice.hint: Check the date of each choice against March 1953. Then ask which one was a response to the land law the report describes.

practice.stem: The photograph was taken in the context of

options.A: the Bay of Pigs invasion, when Cuban exiles trained by the CIA landed in Cuba
options.B: the U-2 incident, when the Soviets shot down an American spy plane over the Soviet Union
options.C: a crisis that began when U.S. spy planes photographed new launch sites under construction in Cuba
options.D: the Cuban Revolution, when Castro's rebels overthrew the dictator Fulgencio Batista

practice.explanation: In October 1962, U.S. spy planes photographed Soviet missile sites in Cuba. Kennedy demanded that the missiles be removed and used the navy to stop new weapons shipments. The standoff brought the superpowers closer to nuclear war than at any other time in the Cold War.

whyNot.A: The Bay of Pigs invasion was in April 1961. The labels point to missile launch sites, not an invasion.
whyNot.B: The U-2 was shot down over the Soviet Union in 1960. This photograph shows Cuba in 1962.
whyNot.D: Castro's rebels won in January 1959. Cuba's Soviet nuclear missile sites were built later.

practice.hint: Look at the date and the labels. Which choice fits both?

practice.stem: Labels on the photograph such as "former launch positions" were most likely added in order to

options.A: prove to the United Nations that the Soviets had secretly placed missiles in Cuba
options.B: record the damage that U.S. air strikes had done to the missile site during the crisis
options.C: help plan U.S. air strikes against the missiles, which some of Kennedy's advisers had urged
options.D: help U.S. leaders check that the Soviets were taking the missile site apart

practice.explanation: On October 28 Khrushchev agreed to remove the missiles. Castro would not let UN inspectors into Cuba, so U.S. planes kept taking pictures. Labels such as "former launch positions" helped leaders see that the missiles were being removed.

whyNot.A: U.S. officials did show photos at the UN in October 1962 to prove the missiles were there. But this photo is dated November 1 and labels "former" launch positions, so it shows the missiles leaving.
whyNot.B: The United States did not carry out the proposed air strikes. Taken after the October 28 agreement, this photograph was used to check the removal of Soviet missiles.
whyNot.C: Some advisers urged air strikes in October. By November 1 Khrushchev had agreed to remove the missiles, and the labels show where missiles used to be.

practice.hint: Compare the date in the title box with what happened during the crisis in October 1962. Which purpose fits a photograph taken on that date?

practice.stem: The missile site in the photograph is evidence of which effect of the Cold War?

options.A: the deployment of Soviet nuclear weapons in the Caribbean as part of the superpower arms race
options.B: the founding of NATO and the Warsaw Pact as rival alliances in Europe
options.C: the use of local fighters, such as Cuban exiles, to fight the superpowers' battles in Latin America
options.D: a thaw in relations between the superpowers after Stalin's death in 1953

practice.explanation: In 1962 the Soviet Union placed nuclear missiles in Cuba, close to the United States. This brought the arms race to the Caribbean and created one of the most dangerous crises of the Cold War.

whyNot.B: These alliances were real, but they were in Europe. The photograph shows missiles in Cuba.
whyNot.C: The CIA did use Cuban exiles at the Bay of Pigs in 1961, but this photo shows a Soviet missile site, not exile fighters.
whyNot.D: There was a short thaw after Stalin died, but this missile site shows a dangerous crisis, not a thaw.

practice.hint: Look at the place named in the title box and the kind of site it labels. Which choice does the photograph itself show?

practice.stem: Gandhi made this statement in the context of

options.A: the Quit India movement, when Congress demanded that Britain leave India at once during the Second World War
options.B: the partition of British India into the separate states of India and Pakistan
options.C: the Sepoy Rebellion, when Indian soldiers rose up against the East India Company
options.D: a mass campaign in which Indians boycotted British courts, schools, and cloth to protest British rule

practice.explanation: After the Amritsar massacre of 1919, Gandhi and the Congress asked Indians to stop using British courts, schools, and cloth. In 1922 a crowd killed policemen in the village of Chauri Chaura. Gandhi stopped the campaign, and soon after he was arrested.

whyNot.A: The Quit India movement began in 1942, twenty years after this trial.
whyNot.B: Partition took place in 1947, twenty-five years later.
whyNot.C: The Sepoy Rebellion took place in 1857, long before Gandhi's public life began.

practice.hint: Look at the date of the trial. Which choice describes events in India in the early 1920s?

practice.stem: Which of the following best states Gandhi's main argument in the last paragraph?

options.A: People should refuse to support unjust rule, but without violence and while accepting punishment.
options.B: Indians should support the British Empire in wartime in return for self-rule later.
options.C: Violence against officials is justified when a government breaks its promises.
options.D: Indians should rebuild their cottage industries and spinning wheels instead of taking part in politics.

practice.explanation: Gandhi says non-cooperation with evil is a duty. But he says it requires "complete abstention from violence," and those who disobey must accept the penalty.

whyNot.B: Gandhi says he has lost faith in British rule. He does not offer to support the empire.
whyNot.C: Gandhi says violent non-cooperation "only multiplies evil."
whyNot.D: Gandhi mentions cottage industry as a sign of harm done by British rule, but his argument is about non-cooperation.

practice.hint: Reread the last paragraph. What two conditions does Gandhi place on non-cooperation?

practice.stem: Gandhi's methods are most similar to those of

options.A: Ho Chi Minh's Viet Minh in the war against French rule in Vietnam
options.B: Martin Luther King Jr. in the civil rights movement in the United States
options.C: the Mau Mau fighters who rose up against British rule in Kenya in the 1950s
options.D: the National Liberation Front (FLN) in Algeria's fight against France

practice.explanation: King studied Gandhi's ideas. Like Gandhi, he led boycotts and marches, refused to use violence, and was willing to go to jail. For many years Nelson Mandela's African National Congress also used nonviolent protest.

whyNot.A: The Viet Minh fought a guerrilla war against the French from 1946 to 1954.
whyNot.C: The Mau Mau used armed attacks in the 1950s, and the British answered with harsh force.
whyNot.D: The FLN fought an eight-year war against France.

practice.hint: Think about how each leader or group fought for change. Which one matches what Gandhi says about violence?

practice.stem: Source 1 was passed in the context of

options.A: the Mau Mau uprising, in which Kikuyu fighters attacked British settlers and officials in Kenya
options.B: a war in Algeria, where nationalists fought to drive out French rule and French settlers
options.C: a nationalist campaign led by Kwame Nkrumah, whose party won elections in the Gold Coast in the 1950s
options.D: the Berlin Conference, at which European powers agreed on rules for dividing up Africa

practice.explanation: In 1949 Kwame Nkrumah founded the Convention People's Party, which led strikes and boycotts against British rule. His party won elections in 1951, 1954, and 1956, and Britain agreed to independence. On March 6, 1957, the Gold Coast became Ghana, one of the first African colonies south of the Sahara to win independence.

whyNot.A: The Mau Mau uprising took place in Kenya, in East Africa. Source 1 is about the Gold Coast, in West Africa.
whyNot.B: The war in Algeria was fought against France. Source 1 is a British law about the Gold Coast.
whyNot.D: The Berlin Conference met in 1884–1885, when Europeans were taking over Africa, not giving it up.

practice.hint: Check the date of each choice against 1957. Then ask which one helped bring about this British law.

practice.stem: Which of the following best describes a difference between the two sources?

options.A: Source 1 was adopted by an international organization, while Source 2 was passed by a national parliament.
options.B: Source 1 calls colonial rule a denial of human rights, while Source 2 praises colonial powers for preparing their colonies.
options.C: Source 1 gives independence to one colony through a law of the ruling power, while Source 2 demands it for colonial peoples everywhere.
options.D: Source 1 describes an armed revolt against Britain, while Source 2 describes a peaceful transfer of power in Ghana.

practice.explanation: The Act records the legal side of a negotiated transfer shaped by nationalist organizing and election victories in the Gold Coast. The UN declaration calls for independence across the colonial world and rejects lack of "preparedness" as a reason for delay.

whyNot.A: This reverses them. Britain's Parliament passed Source 1, and the UN General Assembly adopted Source 2.
whyNot.B: Source 1 says nothing about human rights. It is Source 2 that calls colonial rule "a denial of fundamental human rights."
whyNot.D: Source 1 describes no revolt; it is a law about handing over power. Source 2 does not mention Ghana.

practice.hint: Check each choice against both sources. Who passed each one, and how many places does each cover?

practice.stem: Which of the following developments would best support Source 2's belief that "the process of liberation is irresistible"?

options.A: In 1974–1975, after long wars, Portugal gave up Angola, Mozambique, and its other African colonies.
options.B: In 1965 the white-minority government of Rhodesia broke away from Britain to keep the Black majority out of power.
options.C: In 1966, South Africa rejected the United Nations decision to end its mandate over South West Africa (now Namibia) and continued to govern the territory.
options.D: Britain kept Bermuda, whose voters turned down independence in a 1995 vote.

practice.explanation: Portugal fought long wars against independence movements in its African colonies during the 1960s and early 1970s. These wars helped bring down Portugal's dictatorship in 1974. The new government recognized Guinea-Bissau's independence in 1974, and Mozambique and Angola became independent in 1975. These events support the declaration's belief that colonial rule would end.

whyNot.B: Rhodesia's unilateral declaration was meant to preserve white-minority power. It did not establish majority rule.
whyNot.C: This describes resistance to decolonization in 1966. It does not describe colonial rule ending.
whyNot.D: Bermuda's people chose to stay tied to Britain. That does not show colonial rule being swept away.

practice.hint: For each choice, decide whether colonial rule is ending or holding on.

practice.stem: Which of the following best describes a similarity between the two sources?

options.A: Both describe the fighting as part of a worldwide struggle against communism.
options.B: Both were approved by a vote of the members of an international organization.
options.C: Both ask outsiders to help one side in a conflict to protect the peace of the region around it.
options.D: Both ask the U.S. Congress to send money to fighters who oppose their own government.

practice.explanation: The Security Council asked UN members to help South Korea "repel the armed attack" and restore peace "in the area." Reagan asked Congress to help rebels stop a government that, he said, threatened "its democratic neighbors." One conflict was in Asia and one in the Americas, but in both, outside powers backed one side in a local war.

whyNot.A: Reagan calls Nicaragua's government a "Communist menace," but the resolutions do not mention communism.
whyNot.B: The resolutions were adopted by votes in the Security Council. Reagan's speech was his own appeal to Americans.
whyNot.D: Reagan asks Congress for $100 million for the rebels. The resolutions ask UN members to help South Korea's government.

practice.hint: Check each choice against both sources. A similarity must be true of Source 1 and of Source 2.

practice.stem: The absence of the Soviet Union noted at the end of Source 1 is best explained by

options.A: the "Uniting for Peace" resolution, which let the General Assembly act when the Security Council was blocked
options.B: a Soviet boycott of the Security Council to protest that Nationalist China, not Communist China, held China's seat
options.C: the Soviet Union's decision to leave the United Nations, as Germany and Japan had left the League of Nations
options.D: Stalin's death, which left Soviet diplomats without orders from Moscow

practice.explanation: In January 1950 the Soviet delegate walked out of the Security Council. The Soviets demanded that Mao's new government take China's seat, which Chiang Kai-shek's Nationalist government still held. Because the Soviets were absent, they could not veto the resolutions on Korea. They returned in August 1950.

whyNot.A: The General Assembly passed "Uniting for Peace" in November 1950, months after these votes, after the Soviets had come back to the Council.
whyNot.C: Germany and Japan did leave the League in 1933, but the Soviet Union stayed in the United Nations throughout the Cold War.
whyNot.D: Stalin died in 1953, three years after these resolutions.

practice.hint: Check the date of each choice against June 1950.

practice.stem: Reagan's statement "I'm not talking about American troops" is best understood in the context of

options.A: debates in Congress over the cost of keeping U.S. forces stationed in Western Europe
options.B: widespread concern about another prolonged overseas ground war after the Vietnam War
options.C: efforts to negotiate limits on nuclear weapons deployed in Europe
options.D: efforts to expand trade and diplomatic ties with Communist China

practice.explanation: The Vietnam War caused heavy losses and deep divisions in the United States. More than 58,000 Americans died. Afterward, many Americans feared another long ground war, so Reagan stressed aid to local fighters instead of U.S. troops.

whyNot.A: Debates over troops in Europe were about NATO's costs, not about sending soldiers to fight in Central America.
whyNot.C: Arms talks in Europe concerned nuclear missiles, not ground troops in Nicaragua.
whyNot.D: Ties with China grew from the 1970s, but they do not explain Reagan's promise about troops in Central America.

practice.hint: Reagan says troops "are not needed." Which choice explains why Americans in 1986 might worry that they would be?

practice.stem: Which of the following conclusions is best supported by the table?

options.A: Korean-born people were the largest of the four groups in the table in 1980 and in 1990.
options.B: The Cuban-born population grew faster during the 1980s than it had during the 1960s.
options.C: The number of Vietnam-born people in the United States fell between 1980 and 2000.
options.D: The Philippine-born population grew more than tenfold between 1960 and 2000.

practice.explanation: Ten times 104,843 is about 1 million. By 2000 there were 1,369,070 Philippine-born people, so the group grew more than ten times.

whyNot.A: In both 1980 and 1990 the Korean-born group was smaller than the Cuban-born and Philippine-born groups.
whyNot.B: The Cuban-born group grew by about 360,000 in the 1960s and by about 130,000 in the 1980s.
whyNot.C: It rose from about 231,000 to about 988,000.

practice.hint: Test each choice against the numbers in the table, one row at a time.

practice.stem: The growth of the Philippine-born population shown in the table is best explained by

options.A: the Green Revolution, which raised rice harvests in the Philippines in the 1960s and 1970s
options.B: changes in U.S. immigration law combined with family, work, and school ties from the colonial period
options.C: the Japanese occupation of the Philippines during the Second World War
options.D: the Vietnam War, which sent large numbers of refugees from Southeast Asia to the United States

practice.explanation: The United States ruled the Philippines from 1898 to 1946. That created ties through English, schools, military service, and work. A 1965 U.S. law ended rules that had kept out most Asian immigrants, and family ties and demand for workers helped Filipino migration grow. Like Algerians who moved to France and South Asians who moved to Britain, they moved to the country that had once ruled them.

whyNot.A: Bigger harvests gave people more food at home. They do not explain why Filipinos moved to the United States.
whyNot.C: The occupation ended in 1945, long before most of the growth shown in the table.
whyNot.D: Refugees from the Vietnam War came mainly from Vietnam, Laos, and Cambodia, not the Philippines.

practice.hint: Ask of each choice: would it make people move to the United States in particular? Check the dates, too.

practice.stem: Which development best explains the largest decade-to-decade increase in the Cuban-born population shown in the table?

options.A: the Bracero Program, which brought workers from Mexico to farms in the United States
options.B: the Mariel boatlift, when Castro let more than 100,000 Cubans leave by boat
options.C: the Spanish-American War, after which Cuba came under U.S. control
options.D: the Cuban Revolution, after which many Cubans who opposed Castro's government left

practice.explanation: The largest increase shown came between 1960 and 1970, when the Cuban-born population rose from 79,150 to 439,048. Castro took power in 1959 and built a communist state allied with the Soviet Union. Hundreds of thousands of Cubans, many from the middle and upper classes, left for the United States in the 1960s.

whyNot.A: The Bracero Program brought Mexican farm workers, not Cubans, to the United States.
whyNot.B: The Mariel boatlift took place in 1980, after the years in question.
whyNot.C: The Spanish-American War was fought in 1898, long before 1960.

practice.hint: Check the date of each choice against the decade when the big jump happened.

practice.stem: Both sources describe

options.A: refugees fleeing communist governments in Eastern Europe that had been set up with Soviet help
options.B: migrants moving from former colonies to Britain in search of factory work
options.C: people driven from their homes by the Korean War
options.D: mass displacement tied to the end of British rule and fights over new states and borders

practice.explanation: Britain left India in 1947 and Palestine in 1948. In South Asia, about 10 to 15 million people crossed the new border between India and Pakistan. In Palestine, about 700,000 Palestinian Arabs fled or were expelled during the conflict of 1947–1949. That displacement began before Israel declared independence in May 1948 and continued afterward.

whyNot.A: Neither source mentions communism or the Soviet Union.
whyNot.B: Both sources describe people fleeing violence within the region, not moving to Britain for work.
whyNot.C: The Korean War did drive millions from their homes, but in Korea. These sources describe South Asia and Palestine.

practice.hint: Ask what the people in both sources have in common: who is moving, when, and why?

practice.stem: The Indian government's request for U.S. planes in Source 1 most likely reflects

options.A: the decision of India's new government to join the U.S. side in the Cold War in return for military aid
options.B: the struggle of a newly independent government to protect and move huge numbers of refugees with few resources of its own
options.C: Pakistan's appeal for outside help in its war with India over Kashmir
options.D: the Indian National Congress's demand, made during the Quit India movement, that Britain leave India at once

practice.explanation: Britain left India only seven weeks before this telegram. The new Indian government had to protect millions of people crossing the new border, but it had few working planes. Estimates of the dead in the Partition violence range from about 200,000 to 2 million.

whyNot.A: India stayed out of the Cold War blocs. Nehru later became a leader of the Non-Aligned Movement.
whyNot.C: The telegram concerns India's request to move refugees out of the North-West Frontier Province, not a Pakistani request about Kashmir.
whyNot.D: The Quit India movement began in 1942. By October 1947 Britain had already left.

practice.hint: Look at what the Prime Minister asks for, and why the refugees cannot travel on their own.

practice.stem: According to Source 2, Israel and the Arab states disagreed mainly about

options.A: who had caused the refugee problem and whether refugees should return home or be resettled
options.B: whether the city of Jerusalem should be placed under international control
options.C: whether the United Nations should take over the government of Palestine for a period of years
options.D: whether Palestinian Arabs should have their own state, as the UN partition plan of 1947 had proposed

practice.explanation: The paper reports disputes over who was responsible and over return versus resettlement. Most Arab states refused to resettle the refugees for good (Transjordan was the exception) and wanted them allowed to go home, as the UN had resolved in December 1948. Israel blamed the Arab invasion and wanted resettlement. The paper gives U.S. officials' account of the governments' positions. It does not present the refugees' own views.

whyNot.B: Jerusalem's future was argued over in these years, but point 3 does not mention it.
whyNot.C: The paper does not discuss a UN government for Palestine.
whyNot.D: The UN plan of 1947 did call for an Arab state, but point 3 is about the refugees, not about a state.

practice.hint: Reread point 3. Which choice does that paragraph actually discuss?

practice.stem: The Soviet war in Afghanistan contributed to the end of the Cold War mainly by

options.A: leading the United States and many of its allies to boycott the 1980 Olympic Games in Moscow
options.B: leading the Soviet Union to sign the SALT I agreements limiting certain strategic weapons systems
options.C: costing the Soviet Union money and lives at a time when its economy was already weak
options.D: giving the Soviet Union a warm-water port on the Indian Ocean

practice.explanation: About 15,000 Soviet soldiers died in Afghanistan, and the war cost huge sums. Many Soviet citizens turned against it. Gorbachev decided to bring the troops home, and they left in 1988–1989.

whyNot.A: The United States did boycott the 1980 Olympics, but the boycott did not weaken the Soviet Union the way the long, costly war did.
whyNot.B: The SALT I agreements were signed in 1972, seven years before the invasion.
whyNot.D: Afghanistan has no coastline, and the Soviets gained no port there.

practice.hint: Check the date of each choice against the war (1979–1989). Then ask which one weakened the Soviet Union itself.

practice.stem: U.S. aid to the Afghan rebels described in Source 1 is an example of

options.A: collective security, in which the United Nations sent troops from many countries to stop an invasion
options.B: détente, in which the superpowers worked together to reduce tensions
options.C: proxy warfare, in which a power supports local forces fighting a rival or that rival's allies
options.D: nonalignment, in which a country refused to take sides in the Cold War

practice.explanation: The Soviet Union sent its own troops and supported Afghanistan's government. The United States supported Afghan groups fighting that government and Soviet forces, without sending its own army. The conflict combined direct Soviet intervention with proxy competition. Angola and Nicaragua also saw proxy wars.

whyNot.A: The UN did not send troops to Afghanistan. Aid went secretly through Pakistan.
whyNot.B: The invasion further weakened détente, the effort to ease Cold War tensions.
whyNot.D: The United States, Saudi Arabia, and Pakistan clearly took a side against the Soviets.

practice.hint: Who did the fighting, and who supplied the weapons and money?

practice.stem: Al Qaeda, as described in the two sources, is an example of

options.A: a movement that used violence against civilians to pursue political goals
options.B: a nationalist movement that fought to win independence from a European colonial power
options.C: a political party that won elections and then ruled as a one-party state
options.D: an alliance of oil-producing countries that raised prices to gain political power

practice.explanation: Source 1 shows al Qaeda's founding at the end of the Soviet-Afghan war. Source 2 shows what it did next: the bombings of two U.S. embassies in Kenya and Tanzania in 1998 killed more than 200 people, most of them Africans. In 2001 al Qaeda carried out the September 11 attacks. Other movements of the period, such as the Shining Path in Peru, also used violence against civilians.

whyNot.B: Al Qaeda's founders were not fighting for one country's independence. Source 1 says they planned a base for "future jihad" in many places.
whyNot.C: Al Qaeda did not run in elections or govern a country. It was a secret network that, Source 2 says, the Taliban sheltered.
whyNot.D: That describes OPEC, a group of governments. Al Qaeda was a private network of fighters.

practice.hint: Reread the end of Source 1 and the first two paragraphs of Source 2. What did al Qaeda plan, and what did it do?

practice.stem: Pinochet's rule in Chile, as described in the report, is an example of

options.A: a democratic government that came to power through free and fair elections in 1973
options.B: a military government that met opposition with harsh force, deepening conflict
options.C: a communist government that the Soviet Union helped bring to power
options.D: a socialist government that took over foreign-owned copper mines for the nation

practice.explanation: Pinochet's forces arrested tens of thousands of people. More than 3,000 people were killed or forcibly disappeared under Pinochet's dictatorship. Like Franco in Spain and Idi Amin in Uganda, Pinochet met opposition with force.

whyNot.A: Pinochet's army overthrew Allende, who had been elected.
whyNot.C: Pinochet was anti-communist, and the United States supported his government.
whyNot.D: Allende's government nationalized the major copper mines in 1971. They stayed state-owned under Pinochet, although his government promoted free-market policies in many other areas.

practice.hint: How did Pinochet come to power, and how did his officers treat opponents?

practice.stem: U.S. actions in Chile described in the report were most similar to U.S. actions in which of the following?

options.A: Iran, where the CIA helped overthrow Prime Minister Mohammad Mosaddegh
options.B: West Germany, where the United States paid for rebuilding through the Marshall Plan
options.C: Japan, where U.S. officials wrote a democratic constitution after the war
options.D: Korea, where U.S. troops fought under the United Nations flag

practice.explanation: In Iran in 1953, the CIA and Britain helped overthrow Mosaddegh, who had taken over Iran's oil industry; he had been chosen by Iran's elected parliament. In Chile the CIA funded Allende's opponents and tried to block him from taking office in 1970. Both were secret U.S. actions against leaders seen as threats. This report alone does not show that the CIA directed Chile's 1973 coup.

whyNot.B: Marshall Plan aid was open economic help, not a secret effort to remove a government.
whyNot.C: In Japan the United States openly occupied a defeated country. It did not secretly work against an elected leader.
whyNot.D: In Korea, U.S. troops fought openly in a war. In Chile the CIA acted in secret.

practice.hint: Reread the report. What kind of action did the United States take in Chile, and against whom? Then compare each choice.

practice.stem: A historian could use this report most directly to investigate which question?

options.A: Which hardships most affected Chilean families during military rule?
options.B: How did the CIA describe its contacts with Chile's military government?
options.C: How did rural and urban Chileans differ in their responses to Pinochet?
options.D: What did Chilean political prisoners consider the lasting effects of imprisonment?

practice.explanation: The report was prepared to explain CIA activities to Congress. It directly addresses the agency's contacts, including the officers who were "contacts or agents of the CIA." To study Chileans' experiences, historians would also need Chilean testimony, local records, and truth commission reports.

whyNot.A: The report says little about Chilean families' daily lives. That question needs Chilean testimony and records.
whyNot.C: The report does not compare groups of Chileans. That question needs local records and Chilean voices.
whyNot.D: The report does not include prisoners' own accounts. That question needs their testimony and truth commission reports.

practice.hint: Think about who wrote the report and for whom. Which question could it answer from its own evidence?

practice.stem: The "new policy of reform and openness" that Reagan mentions refers to

options.A: Khrushchev's de-Stalinization, which freed many prisoners from labor camps
options.B: Brezhnev's détente, which led to arms-control treaties with the West
options.C: Gorbachev's reforms known as perestroika and glasnost
options.D: Deng Xiaoping's market reforms in the People's Republic of China

practice.explanation: Gorbachev became the Soviet leader in 1985. Glasnost ("openness") let people speak and write more freely. Perestroika ("rebuilding") tried to fix the economy by loosening state control.

whyNot.A: Khrushchev's reforms came in the 1950s. Reagan speaks of what Moscow is doing "now," in 1987.
whyNot.B: Détente focused on relations between states. Reagan is referring to Gorbachev's reforms within the Soviet Union.
whyNot.D: Deng's reforms took place in China. Reagan is talking about Moscow.

practice.hint: Reread the sentence with "new policy." Where is the policy coming from, and in what year is Reagan speaking?

practice.stem: Reagan's purpose in contrasting the West's prosperity with "failure" in the Communist world was most likely to

options.A: announce that the United States would send food aid to the Soviet Union
options.B: persuade West Germans to accept more American nuclear missiles aimed at the Soviet Union
options.C: praise East Germany's government for letting more of its citizens visit the West
options.D: argue that freedom brings prosperity and push Soviet leaders to go further with reform

practice.explanation: Reagan spoke to people on both sides of the Wall. He said the West's wealth proved that freedom worked. He challenged Gorbachev to show that his reforms were real by opening the Wall.

whyNot.A: Reagan says the Soviet Union "cannot feed itself," but he offers no food aid in this speech.
whyNot.B: American missiles had been placed in West Germany in 1983. In this part of the speech Reagan compares how people live under freedom and under communism.
whyNot.C: Reagan does not praise East Germany's rulers. He calls for the Wall to be torn down.

practice.hint: Whom does Reagan address at the end of the third paragraph, and what does he ask for?

practice.stem: The Strategic Defense Initiative is most closely associated with which pressure on Soviet leaders during the 1980s?

options.A: the cost of the war in Afghanistan, where Soviet troops fought rebels armed partly by the United States
options.B: the perceived cost of keeping up with U.S. military research while Soviet economic growth slowed
options.C: a 1987 treaty in which both superpowers agreed to remove their intermediate-range nuclear missiles
options.D: a rise in world oil prices that brought the Soviet Union large profits from its oil exports

practice.explanation: SDI paid for research on ways to shoot down missiles. The proposed shield was never built as planned. But Soviet leaders worried about U.S. technology and the cost of competing with it while their economy grew slowly. Military costs were one of several pressures on the Soviet system.

whyNot.A: The Afghan war also strained Soviet resources, but it does not explain the pressure created by the military research program named in the question.
whyNot.C: The 1987 INF Treaty required both sides to eliminate ground-launched missiles with ranges of 500 to 5,500 kilometers. It removed missiles; SDI was about building new defenses.
whyNot.D: High oil prices in the 1970s helped the Soviet economy, but prices fell in the 1980s. SDI was about weapons, not oil.

practice.hint: Reread the sentence about the Strategic Defense Initiative. What kind of program was it, and what would it cost a rival to match?

practice.stem: Gorbachev's statement that "freedom of choice is a universal principle that should allow of no exceptions" contributed most directly to which development?

options.A: the Soviet invasion of Czechoslovakia in 1968 to end the reforms of the Prague Spring
options.B: the Chernobyl nuclear disaster, which made many Soviet citizens distrust their government
options.C: the Chinese government's use of troops to end the Tiananmen Square protests in 1989
options.D: the fall of communist governments in Eastern Europe in 1989, when Soviet troops did not step in to save them

practice.explanation: Earlier Soviet leaders had sent tanks to keep communist governments in power, as in Hungary in 1956 and Czechoslovakia in 1968. Gorbachev said each people could choose its own path. In 1989 Poles, Hungarians, East Germans, Czechs, and others pushed out their communist rulers, and the Soviet army stayed in its bases. The Berlin Wall opened in November 1989.

whyNot.A: This happened twenty years earlier and did the opposite: Soviet troops ended a country's free choice.
whyNot.B: Chernobyl happened in 1986, two years before this speech. It was an accident, not a people's choice.
whyNot.C: China's government acted on its own, and it crushed the protests. The Soviet Union did not control China.

practice.hint: Check the date of each choice. Then ask which one fits the idea of letting each people choose.

practice.stem: A historian studying how ordinary Soviet citizens felt about perestroika would find this speech limited mainly because

options.A: it gives the Soviet leader's own claims, made to a world audience, about what his people thought
options.B: it describes radical economic reforms without giving any measurements of changes in production
options.C: it announces military reductions without reporting how NATO governments responded
options.D: it discusses relations among the Soviet republics without tracing their earlier history

practice.explanation: Gorbachev says that "all our peoples and all generations of citizens" support perestroika. A leader speaking to the world wants his reforms to look popular. To learn what ordinary people thought, a historian would look at letters, surveys, protests, and elections, such as the 1989 vote in which many party officials lost.

whyNot.B: Missing production data limits a study of the reforms' economic results, but it does not explain why the speech is weak evidence of citizens' opinions.
whyNot.C: NATO governments' reactions would show foreign responses, not Soviet citizens' views.
whyNot.D: The republics' earlier history would add context, but it would not show how citizens felt about the reforms in 1988.

practice.hint: Ask what kinds of evidence would show how ordinary people felt. Is a leader's speech to the world that kind of evidence?

practice.stem: Which subsequent development most directly challenged Gorbachev's expectation that perestroika would improve relations between the Soviet central government and the republics?

options.A: Gorbachev received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1990 for his part in easing Cold War tensions.
options.B: Soviet voters chose many members of a new Congress of People's Deputies in partly free elections in 1989.
options.C: The Soviet Union broke apart into fifteen separate countries at the end of 1991, about three years later.
options.D: The last Soviet troops left Afghanistan in February 1989.

practice.explanation: Gorbachev described reform as a way to improve relations between the center and the republics within the Soviet Union. Instead, independence movements grew, from the Baltic states to Ukraine, and the Union dissolved in December 1991, showing that those relationships had broken down.

whyNot.A: The prize honored Gorbachev's foreign policy. It does not show trouble between Moscow and the republics.
whyNot.B: These elections were part of the "democratic reform" Gorbachev describes. They do not by themselves show relations between Moscow and the republics breaking down.
whyNot.D: Bringing the troops home was Gorbachev's own decision. It does not show his reforms losing strength.

practice.hint: Reread Gorbachev's claim. Then check the date and the result of each choice.

exam.title: Unit 8 Practice Exam: Cold War and Decolonization
exam.directions: Each set of questions refers to a source: a primary source, a historian's writing, an image, or data. For each question, choose the best answer. Use the source and your knowledge of world history from c. 1900 to the present. There is no penalty for guessing. Some sources use historical labels or insulting descriptions of other peoples and religions; these words show the writers' views.

questions.stem: Truman's statement that Great Britain was "reducing or liquidating its commitments in several parts of the world" is best understood in the context of

options.A: Britain's defeat in the Suez crisis, which showed that it could no longer act alone as a great power
options.B: the economic strain of the Second World War, which also led Britain to give up its rule over India
options.C: the Berlin Blockade, which forced Britain to spend heavily on an airlift to supply West Berlin
options.D: Britain's decision to join the European Economic Community and focus on trade in Europe

rationales.A: Incorrect. The Suez crisis came in 1956, nine years after this speech.
rationales.B: Correct. Britain came out of the war deeply in debt. In 1947 it pulled back from Greece and Turkey and gave up India, and in 1948 it left Palestine.
rationales.C: Incorrect. The Berlin Blockade began in June 1948, more than a year after this speech.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Britain joined the European Economic Community in 1973.

questions.explanation: The war left Britain with huge debts and a weak economy. It could no longer pay to defend its interests around the world. The United States stepped in to take Britain's place in Greece and Turkey.

questions.stem: Truman's description of two "alternative ways of life" was most likely meant to

options.A: warn Americans that the Soviet army was about to invade Greece and Turkey across their northern borders
options.B: persuade Congress that aiding Greece and Turkey was part of a global fight against communism
options.C: ask the United Nations to send peacekeeping troops to Greece's northern border
options.D: explain why the United States would stay neutral in the fighting inside Greece

rationales.A: Incorrect. Truman speaks of armed Communist fighters inside Greece and of "outside pressures," not of an invasion by the Soviet army.
rationales.B: Correct. Truman spoke to Congress to win $400 million in aid. Framing the choice as freedom against oppression made the aid seem necessary.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Truman asks Congress for U.S. aid. He does not ask the UN for troops.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Truman asks for aid to the Greek government against armed Communists, which is taking a side.

questions.explanation: Truman wanted Americans to accept a new role in the world. He described a contest between free societies and societies run by a minority through terror. This idea, called the Truman Doctrine, guided U.S. policy for decades.

questions.stem: The policy Truman announced was most directly carried further by which of the following?

options.A: the Marshall Plan's aid to Western Europe and the founding of NATO
options.B: the Baruch Plan, which proposed that an international agency control atomic energy
options.C: U.S. recognition of the new People's Republic of China as China's government
options.D: the Good Neighbor Policy, which promised that the United States would not send troops into Latin America

rationales.A: Correct. The Marshall Plan (1948) gave Western Europe about $13 billion, and NATO (1949) joined the United States and Western Europe in a military alliance. Both aimed to contain Soviet power.
rationales.B: Incorrect. The Baruch Plan was offered in June 1946, before this speech, and the Soviets turned it down.
rationales.C: Incorrect. The United States refused to recognize Communist China until 1979.
rationales.D: Incorrect. The Good Neighbor Policy dates from 1933, before the Cold War. It did not carry Truman's policy further.

questions.explanation: Truman's promise to "support free peoples" became the policy of containment. Aid to Greece and Turkey came first. The United States then expanded containment through Marshall Plan aid beginning in 1948 and NATO's creation in 1949.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes a difference between the two sources?

options.A: Khrushchev offers to remove the missiles from Cuba, while Kennedy rejects his offer and calls for an invasion of the island.
options.B: Khrushchev links the missiles in Cuba to U.S. missiles in Turkey, while Kennedy wants Cuba settled separately.
options.C: Khrushchev calls the weapons in Cuba offensive, while Kennedy calls them defensive.
options.D: Khrushchev wants the two leaders to settle the crisis alone, while Kennedy turns to the United Nations.

rationales.A: Incorrect. Kennedy says the key parts of Khrushchev's proposals "seem generally acceptable," and he offers "assurances against an invasion of Cuba."
